Photograph: CJ Gunther/The Boston Herald via AP Massachusetts Lindsay Clancy murder trial: toxicologist testifies about medications found in defendant’s blood Variety of prescriptions were found in blood of mother accused of strangling her three children, court hears Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email Edward Helmore Wed 5 Aug 2026 19.27 EDT First published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 12.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of killing her three children in January 2023, continued on Wednesday with a forensic toxicologist testifying to the variety and concentration of medications found in the defendant’s blood. Justin Brower, a forensic toxicologist with NMS Laboratories, testified that his lab examined the levels of four psychiatric medications detected in Clancy’s blood after she allegedly strangled her children and attempted to take her own life. Those drugs included the antidepressant mirtazapine, the mood stabilizer lamotrigine, the antidepressant trazodone and quetiapine, a drug used to treat schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder. Brower noted that quetiapine could also be prescribed in low doses to treat insomnia. Postpartum psychosis or murder? Trial of mother who killed her kids spotlights mental health Read more Asked if the concentrations of each drug were different from what was prescribed, Brower said the only drug that appeared slightly elevated was quetiapine, but noted that it was not at a “toxic concentration” or “suicidal concentration”. “Usually people take handfuls of pills when they’re trying to harm themselves and take their own life, and this is not consistent with that,” Brower testified. He later testified, upon questioning from Clancy’s defense attorney, that the toxicology results “don’t tell the entire story”. Prosecutors say Clancy acted intentionally when she killed her children Callan, eight months old; Dawson, three years old; and Cora, five years old. Clancy’s defense team says she was a loving mother who was overcome by postpartum psychosis, had undiagnosed bipolar disorder and was on problematic medications. The court has heard from a range of experts for the prosecution, with testimony at times halted when witnesses, including Clancy’s ex-husband, Patrick Clancy, or the defendant have become overwhelmed. On Wednesday, the family’s nanny, Elaine Rossi, was asked on the stand if she’d ever had concerns about Clancy’s care for her children. “Not at all. She was a wonderful mom,’ she said. “I observed a wonderful mom who loved her kids.” If convicted, Clancy faces life in prison without parole. A not-guilty verdict by reason of a lack of criminal responsibility could lead to her being placed in a state mental health facility. On Monday, jurors heard excerpts from Clancy’s journals that revealed her mental struggles including thoughts of suicide and her feeling overwhelmed with motherhood, including her struggles to get her newborn to sleep, going back to work as a labor and delivery nurse, not being able to breastfeed, and feeling disconnected from her children and husband. “I’m so desperate to get a mental break from taking care of everyone that my mind is trying to find something physically wrong with me,” she wrote in an entry on 18 November 2022. The trial has shone a light on significant gaps in the diagnosis and treatment of postpartum psychosis and postpartum depression. Clancy’s attorneys say her condition seemed to worsen on an ever-shifting lineup of psychiatric prescriptions. In the three months before the killings, clinicians prescribed a range of antidepressants, sleep aids, an antipsychotic and other medications while Clancy reported increasingly profound insomnia, anxiety, despair and confusion about what was real, according to a civil lawsuit filed against caregivers that claims they should have recognized that Clancy and her children were at risk. In her diaries, Clancy wrote, “I want help. I want to be well,” and described feeling “incredibly sad and guilty” about not breastfeeding. She also wrote that she was “obsessed” with managing Callan’s sleep and nap schedule. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion “I have crazy brain fog. I feel like I can’t make a plan,” she wrote in another, undated entry. “I live moment to moment waiting for the next nap time. I’m terrified of Cal getting overtired now because I feel can’t help him.” “Hearing him cry for 1 plus hours and not intervening just about killed me,” Clancy wrote, adding that she had told her husband, Patrick, “I want to die.” She also wrote: “I now have horrible insomnia and anxiety which is causing depression. I have no appetite. I don’t know what’s wrong with me. I want help. I want to be well.” Clancy first sought help from a postpartum depression program in late December 2022. She went on to check herself into a psychiatric hospital and later told a psychiatrist that she heard a “man’s voice” in her head telling her to “kill the children so you can kill yourself”. Nineteen days later, after being discharged, she carried out the killings. The defendant is now paralyzed from her attempt to take her own life. When she woke up in hospital and was asked by a forensic psychologist how she felt, she responded: “Horrified.” Dr Jhilam Biswas of Brigham and Women’s hospital testified that Clancy asked “can she have visitors, and where her family is”. The court has also heard from Patrick Clancy, who recounted the medications his former wife was taking, her health and demeanor, and the destructive thoughts she was having. He has said he forgives Lindsay and believes that the killings were motivated purely by her mental health. When the jury heard the anguished 911 call Patrick Clancy made on the night of the killings, several members could be seen holding back tears. He described returning home after collecting medications and a takeout meal to find their home “quiet”. Patrick Clancy went upstairs to find found the door to their bedroom locked. After breaking in, the room was covered in blood and the window was open. His wife was lying on the ground below. She told him she had tried to take her own life. He asked where the children were, and she told him they were in the basement. When emergency services arrived, he ventured downstairs to find their three children with exercise resistance bands around their necks. Duxbury police officer Brian Josephine testified that he heard Patrick scream: “She killed the fucking kids.” Explore more on these topics Massachusetts Mental health US crime news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Beállítom Az elmúlt években 250 millió forint közpénzért adott tanácsokat és utasításokat külföldről a Szemereyné Pataki Klaudia kecskeméti polgármester által megbízott Csapó Ágnes önkormányzati főtanácsadó a hivatalnak és önkormányzati cégeknek – erről beszélt kedden Király József, a Szövetség a Hírös Városért Egyesület képviselője és frakcióvezetője Kecskeméten. A Bács-Kiskun Vármegyei Rendőr-főkapitányság megkeresésünkre megerősítette, hogy Király József önkormányzati képviselő ismeretlen tettes ellen hűtlen kezelés bűntettének gyanúja miatt tett feljelentést. Az ügyben a feljelentés kiegészítését is elrendelték. Király József a KecsUP -nak korábban arról beszélt, hogy Csapó Ágnes külföldön él, és onnan online vagy telefonon keresztül a város különböző gazdasági társaságainak nemcsak tanácsokat, hanem sokszor utasításokat is ad, még vezetői értekezleteken is részt vesz online meeting formában. Király hozzátette, hogy mindezeket azonban nem rögzítik, nincs nyomuk, amit elfogadhatatlannak tart. Csapó Ágnes 2013 és 2018 között a kecskeméti AIPA Alföldi Iparfejlesztési Nonprofit Közhasznú Kft. ügyvezetési feladatait látta el. Érdekeltségébe tartozik továbbá a Budapest Priv-Invest Gazdasági Tanácsadó Kft., Csapó Ágnes és Szemereyné Pataki Klaudia korábban együtt is dolgoztak az AIPA-ban. Szemereyné 2013 májusáig vezette ügyvezetőként a céget, akkor még önkormányzati képviselőként. 2014-ben Kecskemét polgármesterévé választották Szemereynét, 2016-ban pedig az önkormányzat többségi tulajdonába került az AIPA. Király megkérdezte a város polgármesterétől, hogy Csapó Ágnes jelenleg milyen pozíciókat tölt be az önkormányzatnál és a város gazdasági társaságainál. Szemereyné Pataki Klaudia válaszából kiderült, hogy Csapó Ágnes önkormányzati főtanácsadó, havi 1,45 millió forintos fizetéssel. A Királyhoz eljutott munkaköri leírása alapján heti 40 órában, vagyis teljes munkaidőben dolgozik. Király József állítása szerint így nehezen elképzelhető, hogy még annyi más cégnek is tudott szakérteni, tanácsot adni. https://www.politico.eu/article/latvia-d.text: Latvia has detained two of its citizens since June on suspicion of spying for Russia's military intelligence agency and using a private aircraft to surveil an army base hosting NATO forces, authorities said Thursday. Latvia's State Security Service (VDD) said the two Latvian citizens are suspected of collecting information on the Ādaži base — one of Latvia's most important military stations and home to NATO's brigade in the country — as well as military radar systems and the movement of planes. According to the VDD , the pair gathered information for Russia's GRU military intelligence service. One of the suspects even used a private aircraft to conduct reconnaissance and take aerial photographs of the base. Authorities allege that the pair carried out activities that could support Russian intelligence and sabotage groups operating in Latvia. The case comes amid heightened concern across NATO's eastern flank over Russian sabotage and other hybrid operations targeting the government's support for Ukraine. Criminal proceedings were opened on June 27 and the investigation is ongoing. Advertisement Advertisement

Top supplier China sold Algeria US$10.58 billion of goods in 2024, about 22% of everything Algeria imported. Foreign investment Net direct investment from abroad was US$1.54 billion in 2025, about 0.5% of an economy of US$287 billion, as of October 2026. US trade US goods exports to Algeria were US$1.28 billion in 2025 and imports US$2.24 billion, a US deficit of US$959 million. UAE rift Algeria’s foreign ministry cut ties with the United Arab Emirates on 10 September 2026; its defence ministry closed airspace to Emirati aircraft. Borrowing Algeria owed foreign creditors only US$6.9 billion at the end of 2024, about 2.7% of its output. Algeria’s foreign partners fall into three groups: European gas buyers led by Italy and Spain, a Chinese supplier that sells it more goods than any other country, and American, Asian and Gulf energy companies that hold contracts with the state oil and gas firm Sonatrach. As of October 2026 foreign direct investment is small, at US$1.54 billion in 2025, and the state keeps control of the strategic sectors. Open the full Ask Rio Times → Algeria’s Foreign Money at a Glance Algeria is a state-led economy of 47.4 million people and an output of US$287.0 billion in 2025, the World Bank’s figures show as of October 2026. Oil and gas dominate, and the US State Department says hydrocarbons have historically supplied 95% of export revenue and about 40% of government revenue. Foreign money arrives mainly as contracts rather than as ownership. Net direct investment from abroad was US$1.54 billion in 2025 and US$1.30 billion in 2024, which is about 0.5% of output in both years. Foreign borrowing is small too, with external debt of US$6.9 billion at the end of 2024, about 2.7% of that year’s output. The State Department describes the government as historically debt-averse and resistant to foreign financing. Algerians abroad send home more cash than foreign investors bring, with personal remittances of US$1.69 billion in 2025. The wider picture of who runs the economy is in the guide to Algeria’s economy and its key players . Europe, the Gas Customer File photo, 2009. Algiers and its harbour on the Mediterranean coast, seen from the International Space Station. (Photo: NASA astronaut, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons) Europe is the first reason Algeria matters abroad, because pipelines tie Algerian gas fields to Italian and Spanish homes and factories. Eurostat, the European Union’s statistics office, counts 40.1 billion cubic metres of Algerian gas imported by EU countries in 2024. Italy took 23.3 billion cubic metres of it, which was 39% of all the gas Italy imported that year. Spain took 11.7 billion, also 39% of its imports, while Germany took none from Algeria in 2024. Eni, the Italian energy group, calls itself the leading international energy company in the region on its Algeria page. It signed a 30-year production-sharing contract with Sonatrach on 7 July 2025 for the Zemoul El Kbar area of the Berkine Basin, with planned investment of US$1.35 billion. Under a production-sharing contract the foreign company pays the exploration costs and recovers them from the oil or gas it finds, and the rest is split with the state. Eni says the area covers about 4,200 square kilometres and absorbed neighbouring assets that had been under separate contracts. Spain’s main link is the Medgaz pipeline, which runs under the sea from Beni Saf in Algeria to Almería and has carried gas since 2011. Its operator says it raised the line’s capacity by 25% in November 2019. Germany is a newer customer. Sonatrach and the German gas group VNG signed a supply contract on 16 July 2026 during President Abdelmadjid Tebboune’s official visit to Germany, with deliveries to the German market starting on 1 January 2027. The two companies also partner in hydrogen projects called ALTEH2A and SoutH2 Corridor, which aim to produce hydrogen in Algeria for export to Europe. The Czech utility ČEZ, for its part, extended its gas contract with Sonatrach by one year from 1 October 2025, with the gas flowing through the pipeline that links Algeria to Italy. Trade data show how concentrated the buyers are. Of the US$51.9 billion of goods Algeria reported exporting in 2024, Italy took US$12.4 billion (24%), France US$7.6 billion (15%) and Spain US$6.4 billion (12%), according to the United Nations trade database Comtrade. France is also the third-largest source of Algerian imports, at US$3.11 billion in 2024, just behind Italy at US$3.17 billion. For the pipelines and gas politics behind these numbers, see the explainer on Algerian gas and Europe . American Oil Companies and Washington The United States buys more from Algeria than it sells. Census Bureau figures show US goods exports to Algeria of US$1.28 billion in 2025 and imports of US$2.24 billion, a US trade deficit of US$959 million. In the first eight months of 2026 US exports were US$1.00 billion and imports US$1.93 billion, a deficit of US$929 million, as of October 2026. The US deficit with Algeria was US$1.45 billion in 2024 and US$959 million in 2025. American oil firms are courting access to Algerian fields. Sonatrach’s chief executive Nour Eddine Daoudi visited the United States from 12 to 16 October 2026 and met six US energy and oilfield-service companies, ExxonMobil, Halliburton, Devon Energy, Baker Hughes, KBR and Occidental Petroleum, known as Oxy. ExxonMobil signed a memorandum of understanding with Sonatrach in May 2024 to review development of the Ahnet and Gourara basins, which is a preliminary document and not a contract. Oxy has worked with Sonatrach in the Berkine Basin for years and, with Eni and the French group TotalEnergies, signed a hydrocarbon agreement for perimeters 404 and 208 in 2022. Baker Hughes, with the Italian firms Nuovo Pignone International and Tecnimont, won an engineering and construction contract signed in May 2024 for the Boosting III Stage 2 project at the Hassi R’Mel gas field, Sonatrach says. KBR, a US engineering group, has been present in the Algerian energy sector since the early 1980s, the same release adds. The US government’s own view of the business climate is mixed. Its 2025 Investment Climate Statement says a state-dominated economy presents challenges for US businesses, while naming agriculture, information technology, mining, hydrocarbons, renewable energy and healthcare as fields where officials seek US investment. China, the Biggest Supplier China sells Algeria more than any other country. Algeria’s customs data, as collected by Comtrade, show US$10.58 billion of Chinese goods in 2024, which is 22% of Algeria’s US$47.4 billion of imports. China buys far less in return, with US$1.99 billion of Algerian goods in 2024, about 4% of Algeria’s exports. Chinese companies are active in Algerian oil and gas as partners and as contractors. File photo, 2011. A road sign for Arzew, the Mediterranean port town on Algeria’s west coast, with the shoreline beyond. (Photo: Maya-Anaïs Yataghène, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons) Sinopec, the Chinese state oil company, has been present in Algeria since 2002 and works with Sonatrach on the Zarzaitine deposit. On 25 February 2025 the two signed a production-sharing contract for the Hassi Berkane North perimeter, with a projected investment of US$850 million and China’s ambassador Dong Guangli present. On 28 August 2026 Sonatrach and Sinopec signed a memorandum in Beijing covering conventional and unconventional hydrocarbons, complex reservoirs, petrochemicals and helium. A day later Sonatrach signed another memorandum there with the Chinese oilfield-services group Anton on shale-type resources and equipment made locally. Chinese firms also win service work. A consortium of CAIEC and SLPI, two Chinese companies, won two contracts on 25 September 2025 to inspect five gas pipelines with a combined length of 3,576 kilometres, and Sinopec Guangzhou Engineering signed on 17 November 2025 to build a naphtha-treating unit at the Arzew refinery. Russia, Turkey and the Gulf Arms are the clearest Russian link, and they have shrunk. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), an independent research body, ranks Algeria 33rd among world arms importers for 2021 to 2025, with imports down 78% from the peak of 2016 to 2020. SIPRI says Russian arms exports to Algeria fell substantially in that period, and it warns that Algeria is often secretive, so its estimates may be on the low side. Russia also sold Algeria US$2.02 billion of goods in 2024, about 4% of Algerian imports, the UN trade database shows. Turkey combines trade with factories. It was Algeria’s fifth-largest source of imports in 2024 at US$2.57 billion, and it bought US$3.46 billion of Algerian goods. The Turkish steel group Tosyalı runs a complex in Oran that its Algerian website says employs up to 8,000 people and makes it the biggest private-sector employer in Algeria. That figure is the company’s own. The Gulf picture is mixed. Qatar’s telecom group Ooredoo has run a mobile network in Algeria since 2004, and the Saudi company Midad Energy North Africa signed a production-sharing contract with Sonatrach for the Illizi South perimeter on 13 October 2025 with the Saudi ambassador present. Algeria’s foreign ministry announced on 10 September 2026 that it was cutting diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates, saying it had exhausted all means of keeping ties. Algeria’s defence ministry said it closed Algerian airspace from 11 September 2026 to all civil and military aircraft registered in the UAE, with a temporary exemption for commercial flights to and from Algiers airport until the end of 2026. Asian energy firms are also in the field. Thailand’s PTTEP has worked in Algeria since 2002 and signed a memorandum with Sonatrach on 5 October 2026, while Indonesia’s Pertamina signed three service contracts on 22 December 2025 to lift its share of crude oil, condensate and liquefied petroleum gas from the Menzel Ledjmet perimeter. Lenders, Rules and the Investment Climate The International Monetary Fund (IMF), the global crisis lender, is an adviser here rather than a lender. Its 2025 review of Algeria, concluded by its board on 11 September 2025, found the outlook broadly positive but clouded by growing fiscal vulnerabilities. The IMF’s database puts general government gross debt at 52.1% of output in 2025, as of October 2026. Algeria joined the New Development Bank, the lender set up by the BRICS group of large emerging economies, on 19 May 2025, according to the bank’s member list. File photo, 2009. Aerial view of Algiers, with the harbour and the Mediterranean coast in the background. (Photo: LBM1948, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons) The legal framework limits foreign control in key fields. Since 2020 the 51/49 rule, which requires Algerian partners to hold 51% of a project, applies only to named strategic sectors, which are energy, mining, defence, transportation, infrastructure and pharmaceutical manufacturing, the State Department’s investment report says. A 2021 law restored the rule for companies that import goods to resell them. A new investment law replaced the 2016 version in July 2022, and a draft mining law that would let foreign owners hold 80% of a mining project, up from 49%, was still pending as of June 2025, the same report says. Embassies and Diplomats The European Union’s delegation in Algiers is headed by Ambassador Diego Mellado, and China’s ambassador is Dong Guangli, whose embassy lists meetings with Algerian party leaders in October 2026. The US embassy in Algiers has been led since February 2026 by a chargé d’affaires, Mark Schapiro, which is the title of a diplomat who runs a mission when there is no ambassador. Algeria’s ambassador in Washington is Sabri Boukadoum, who spoke at an energy forum in Louisiana on 15 October 2026 alongside Sonatrach’s chief. The forum was organised by the US-Algeria Bus
